questiontext.text:
Explore a randomised forest dataset. Each row represents one tree. Start with a blank graph: choose variables for both axes, then explore colour, point size and treatment panels.

You can download the CSV dataset here or you can also inspect the exact measurements of any tree using the selector in the controls above the graph.

Use the dropdown menus and checkboxes above the plot to choose your visual mappings. Each point is labelled with its Tree_ID. Click a point or use the “Inspect exact measurements” dropdown to see its height, growth and diameter in the information panel in the controls above the graph. The numerical mapping fields below the graph record your selections automatically; please use the visual controls rather than typing into those fields.

generalfeedback.text:
Position: Put height on one axis and annual growth on the other. Read the Tree_ID beside the highest-growth point, then look up its height. The fastest-growing tree is T{@ta_fastest_tree@}, with height {@ta_height_fastest@} m and growth {@ta_growth_fastest@} cm.

Colour: Treatment is categorical: colour distinguishes fertilised and control trees. The maximum growth values are {@ta_control_max@} cm for control trees and {@ta_fert_max@} cm for fertilised trees. These are maxima, not treatment-group means.

Size: Larger circles represent greater trunk diameter. The tallest tree has diameter {@ta_tallest_diameter@} cm, whereas the thickest tree has height {@ta_thickest_height@} m. They are different trees in this variant.

Panels: Faceting by treatment shows the same variables in two separate displays, making within-group patterns easier to inspect. A suitable final graph uses growth on X, height on Y, treatment for colour, diameter for size and treatment panels. Multiple visual properties can encode distinct variables at once.
